module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1207

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/1207](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1207)
- [BMP05] Brass, Peter and Moser, William and Pach, János, *Research problems in discrete geometry*.
  (2005), xii+499.
- [Er80] Erdős, Paul, *A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory*. Ann. Discrete Math.
  (1980), 89-115.
- [PaTa02] Pach, János and Tardos, Gábor, *Isosceles triangles determined by a planar point set*.
  Graphs Combin. (2002), 769--779.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter
open scoped EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos1207

/--
`P d n` is the largest number $m$ such that every set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has an
isosceles-free subset of size at least $m$.
-/
noncomputable def P (d n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {m : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset (ℝ^d), S.card = n ∧
    m = sSup {k : ℕ | ∃ A ⊆ S, (A : Set (ℝ^d)).IsIsoscelesFree ∧ A.card = k}}

/--
Let $P_d(n)$ be such that in any set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ there exist at least $P_d(n)$ many points which do not contain an isosceles triangle. Estimate $P_d(n)$ - in particular, is it true that $$P_2(n)<n^{1-c}$$ for some constant $c>0$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_1207 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, (P 2 n : ℝ) < (n : ℝ) ^ (1 - c) := by
  sorry

end Erdos1207

status_issues.recorded: @[category research open, AMS 52] with `answer(sorry)`; the module references do not cite any resolving work.
status_issues.source_status: Resolved affirmatively. The current erdosproblems.com/1207 page records that Lee, Pohoata and Zhu [LPZ26, arXiv:2607.05374, submitted 6 Jul 2026] proved P_2(n) < n^{1-c} for an absolute constant c > 0, and that this 'answers the main question of Erdős'. The page badge stays OPEN only 'as a general challenge to estimate P_d(n) more generally'. The declaration does not formalize that open-ended part; it formalizes only the concrete P_2 question, which is now answered 'yes'.
status_issues.evidence: Live LaTeX source at https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/1207, fetched 2026-09-23 through r.jina.ai: "A better construction, which proves that $P_2(n)<n^{1-c}$ for some absolute constant $c>0$, was found by Lee, Pohoata, and Zhu (assisted by ChatGPT) \cite{LPZ26}. ... Although this answers the main question of Erdős, I leave this open as a general challenge to estimate $P_d(n)$ more generally." [LPZ26] S. Lee, C. Pohoata, D. G. Zhu, 'The Minkowski grid has robustly many repeated distances', arXiv:2607.05374. Its Corollary (label cor:simultaneous), item (2): "There is an absolute constant δ>0 such that, for every sufficiently large n, there is a single set of n points P⊂ℝ² ... Every subset A⊆P with |A|≥n^{1-δ} contains an isosceles triangle." The paper defines f_iso(n) = min_{|P|=n} α_iso(P) with 'degenerate isosceles triangles (three equally spaced collinear points) also forbidden', which is exactly the Lean `P 2 n`. It says this 'confirms a conjecture by Erdős from 1980 [p. 110]'. The result was also flagged in the forum thread erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1207 (KentaKitamura, 08 Jul 2026). The problem file was added on 2026-09-07, after the preprint. I proved in Lean that the corollary, taken as a hypothesis, implies the theorem's right-hand side `∃ c > 0, ∀ᶠ n in atTop, (P 2 n : ℝ) < n^(1-c)` with c = δ.

reformulations.difference: The source asks for the largest m such that every n-point set in ℝ^d has at least m points with no isosceles triangle. The Lean instead defines `P d n` as `sInf` over n-element Finsets S of `sSup {k | ∃ A ⊆ S, IsIsoscelesFree A ∧ A.card = k}`, i.e. a min over S of the max isosceles-free subset size. `IsIsoscelesFree` also forbids degenerate isosceles triples, where one point is the midpoint of the other two.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For d = 2, ℝ² is infinite, so an n-point set exists for every n. The outer `sInf` therefore ranges over a nonempty set of naturals and is an attained minimum; the `sInf ∅ = 0` default is never reached. Each inner set contains 0 (take A = ∅) and is bounded by n, so its `sSup` is an attained maximum. The minimum over S of the maximum isosceles-free subset size is exactly the greatest m that every S attains. Proved in Lean for every n: `IsGreatest {m | ∀ S : Finset ℝ², S.card = n → ∃ A ⊆ S, (A : Set _).IsIsoscelesFree ∧ m ≤ A.card} (P 2 n)`. Also verified `P 2 1 = 1` and `P 2 3 = 2`; the latter uses a right isosceles triangle. On degenerate triples: the source's remark that d = 1 'is equivalent to finding sets with no three-term arithmetic progressions' shows they count as isosceles. LPZ26 uses the same convention ('degenerate isosceles triangles (three equally spaced collinear points) are also forbidden').

review.notes:
No misformalization found.

Lean experiments, all compiled with no errors against the committed module:
- `P 2 1 = 1`.
- `P 2 3 = 2`.
- `P 2 n` is the `IsGreatest` element of {m | every n-point planar set has an isosceles-free subset of size ≥ m}.
- The Lee–Pohoata–Zhu corollary, taken as a hypothesis, implies the theorem's right-hand side with c = δ.

`EuclideanSpace` distance is the L2 distance, as intended. `#check` shows the statement as `True ↔ …`; that is the repository's default elaboration of `answer(sorry)` at `Prop`, not a defect.

The `answer(sorry)` slot has the same polarity as the source's question ("is it true that P_2(n) < n^{1-c} for some c > 0"), so it is not a negated conjecture.

The `∀ᶠ n in atTop` reading is the intended one. Read as "for all n", the claim fails trivially at n = 1, where P_2(1) = 1 = 1^{1-c}. For some c > 0, it is equivalent to P_2(n) = O(n^{1-c}): shrink c.

Only the concrete P_2 question is formalized; the open-ended "Estimate P_d(n)" is not. That is standard and not a defect.

I could not read Er80 p.110 directly: the Rényi archive PDF is scanned and no OCR tools are available. The erdosproblems.com transcription is the cited ground truth. LPZ26, which cites Er80 p.110 for the same conjecture, agrees with it.

The only actionable item is the stale status above. The formalized main question was answered affirmatively by arXiv:2607.05374 (July 2026), and erdosproblems.com now says so, although the page badge stays OPEN for the general estimation challenge.
